theory.intro: To draw a **distance–time graph**, plot the point reached at the end of each stage and join consecutive points with straight lines. Time goes across, distance goes up.
facts: Time is always on the **horizontal** axis and distance on the **vertical** axis.
Plot the **total** time elapsed and the **total** distance reached at the end of each stage, not the stage's own figures.
A stationary stage is drawn **horizontal** — time passes but the distance reading does not change.
A stage returning towards the start slopes **down**; the line touches the time axis when the traveller is back where they began.
Check the scale on both axes before plotting: one grid line rarely stands for one unit.
If a stage gives a speed and a time rather than a distance, work the distance out with $d=st$ first.
steps: Work out the total time and total distance at the end of each stage.
Plot each of those points on the grid.
Join consecutive points with straight line segments.
